title: How much money do I really need to live?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how much money a person needs to live, based on a HowStuffWorks article by Jane McGrath. They cover the U.S. government poverty threshold (about $10,830 for a single person in 2009 and about $22,050 for a family of four), its origins in Mollie Orshansky's 1960s formula built on food costs multiplied by three, and why that formula is outdated given modern expenses like cars, cable, cell phones and internet. They discuss needs versus wants and relative needs, then practical money-saving tips: clipping coupons, shopping at outlet and discount stores, buying generic brands, cooking at home versus eating out, skipping cable, and saving. The episode closes with a blog plug, a plug for their spoken word album on the economy, and a listener mail segment from Patrick about recurring deja vu episodes with dizzy spells and memory loss.
topics: how much money do you need to live

segments.title: Opening banter and monthly expenses calculator
segments.summary: Hosts joke around, mention the monthly expenses calculator on the site, talk about skipping meals and cutting costs, and introduce the topic and the article by Jane McGrath.

segments.title: Government poverty line and its origins
segments.summary: Chuck explains the government poverty threshold: about $10,830 for a single person and $22,050 for a family of four in 2009. Josh shares that he once lived below it while working as a production assistant in Los Angeles. They explain Mollie Orshansky's 1960s formula, which multiplied the cost of a healthy diet by three based on a 1955 USDA finding that Americans spent about a third of income on food.

segments.title: Why the poverty formula is outdated
segments.summary: The hosts argue the formula has barely changed beyond inflation adjustments for food. Food is now a smaller share of income, and modern expenses such as car loans, cable TV, wireless internet and cell phones were absent when the formula was made.

segments.title: Needs versus wants and relative needs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difference between needs and wants, and the idea of relative needs: keeping up with neighbors and staying competitive in the job market, for example with a cell phone. They also discuss the difficulty of trimming bills like cell phone plans and cable.

segments.title: Frugal living tips: coupons, outlet stores, generics, cooking
segments.summary: Chuck describes his mother raising a family of five on a teacher's salary using coupons and discount and outlet stores. They discuss generic brands like Kroger store brands and Billy Beer, the savings from cooking at home and bringing lunch to work, and the healthier cost of cooking versus fast food. They also mention going without cable and saving money.

segments.title: Savings culture and recession
segments.summary: The hosts say Americans are becoming more frugal and a nation of savers, and they hope the recession passes. They compare themselves to the Depression-era generation.

segments.title: Blog and spoken word album plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote the show's blog and their spoken word album, The Stuff You Should Know Super Stuff Guide to the Economy, available on iTunes.
topics: super Stuff Guide to the Economy

segments.title: Listener mail from Patrick about deja vu
segments.summary: Patrick writes that he has had deja vu episodes with dizziness, mumbling, headaches and brief loss of consciousness since age twelve, occurring in monthly clusters. Doctors ran EEGs and an MRI without an explanation. Chuck urges him to see a neurologist, and Josh jokes about the stigmata theory.
